notes.1a: Most candidates read the scale of the thermometer correctly and stated that room temperature was 23 ° C. The most common incorrect answers were 20.3 ° C and 37 ° C.
notes.1b: The precautions needed to be taken to obtain an accurate value for the highest temperature of the cold/hot water mixture were well known. The most popular correct answers were perpendicular Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2022 viewing of the scale of the thermometer and stirring the water before taking the temperature. Less popular, but equably acceptable correct answers were to ensure that the thermometer is not touching the sides of the beaker and to wait for the thermometer reading to stop rising before reading the temperature. The calculation of the decrease in temperature of the hot water and the increase in temperature of the cold water were almost always correct. Occasionally the unit was missing from the answer, despite the instruction to include the unit being given in the question.
notes.1c: A sizeable minority of candidates were unaware of how to calculate the average value, θ A , of θ H and θ C . Despite the instruction to show the working, many candidates just wrote down the answer for θ . This meant that no credit could be awarded for correct working . (d) Many candidates had difficulty in deciding whether the values of θ A and θ M were sufficiently close to conclude that they were equal within the limits of experimental error. Candidates were often unable to give a convincing justification for their statements. The idea of experimental tolerances, and whether the difference between two measured quantities is close enough to zero for them to be considered equal, was not well understood by most candidates. Generally, if two values differ by 10 per cent or less, the expected answer is “yes, they are the same”. If the values differ by more than 10 per cent the expected answer is “no, they are different”. A calculation should be given to justify the statement made.
notes.1e: Most candidates were able to state two requirements to ensure an accurate result when reading the volume of water in a measuring cylinder. Answers were sometimes too vague, for example “view the measuring cylinder at right angles”, instead of “view the scale reading of the measuring cylinder at right angle” and “take the reading below the meniscus” instead of “take the reading at the bottom of the meniscus”.
notes.2a: The normal to the middle of the mirror was almost always drawn accurately and in the correct place.
notes.2b: Most candidates drew a line 7.0 cm long to represent the incident ray in the correct quadrant of Fig. 2.1 , and at an angle of incidence of α = 30 ° to the normal, as instructed. The most common error was to use the protractor incorrectly and draw a line 7.0 cm long at α = 60 ° . Despite the instruction to label the end of the line with the letter A, the label was often missing.
notes.2c: For accurate ray tracing, the positions of pins P and P should be at least 5.0 cm apart. Most 1 2 candidates suggested a distance greater than this and within the accepted tolerance range of between 5.0 cm and 15.0 cm.
notes.2d: Angle β was usually measured correctly to ± 2 ° , the tolerance allowed for the measurement of the angle. The units of angles were usually included in the table headings. However, some candidates gave ° C as the unit.
notes.2e: The values of ( α + β ) for both angles of incidence α , were almost always calculated correctly.
notes.2f: Only stronger candidates were able to suggest a relationship between the two values of ( α + β ) they had just calculated. These candidates identified that the two values of ( α + β ) were the same (allowing for experimental error). Answers such as that the values of ( α + β ) are close / almost equal / not too far apart, were also accepted.
notes.2g: There were few completely correct answers to this part. Candidates were asked to suggest further values for the angle of incidence α that they could use to extend the investigation. Many correctly suggested values of α > 45 ° (and < 90 ° ), and gained credit. Far fewer suggested any angle α < 30 ° . A sizeable minority of candidates quoted values of α > 90 ° , which showed a lack of understanding of the term angle of incidence.
notes.2h: The practical reasons why the results obtained may not be exactly those that the theory of reflection predicts were not well known. The main difficulty, which was not clear to most candidates, was the difficulty in lining up the pins P 3 and P 4 with the images of P 1 and P 2 so that Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2022 they all appeared exactly one behind the other. Answers such as suggesting that the pins were too thick or that the lines drawn to represent the rays were too thick were also accepted.
notes.3a: The scale reading on the metre ruler at the point where the unloaded metre rule balanced on the pivot was almost always recorded correctly as 48.8 cm.
notes.3b: Only a minority of candidates correctly stated that to obtain an accurate value for the scale reading at balance, it was necessary to view the scale perpendicularly. Many candidates stated that the scale should be viewed at eye level, but this comment was inappropriate here as the scale was being viewed from above and not from the side. –1 (c) The unit for 1 / P caused considerable difficulty, with only stronger candidates giving 1 / N or N . The most common incorrect unit given was N.
notes.3d: Despite the instruction given in the question to start the y -axis at a = 30 cm, many candidates did not do this. There was little evidence of the use of scales that increased in inconvenient increments, such as 3 or 7. Choosing such scales makes the points much harder to plot by candidates and more difficult for the candidates’ plotted points to be checked. There were many excellent, carefully drawn, best-fit lines produced. However, there were many graphs where the attempt at a best-fit line resulted in all points which did not lie on the drawn line being on the same side of the line. A minority of the lines drawn were forced through the origin. There were also some graphs where the points were joined dot-to-dot. The concept of best fit was not well understood by all candidates.
notes.3e: The use of the graph to find the value of a when the ratio 1 / P = 0 was done well by most candidates. The instruction to show clearly on the graph how the necessary information had been obtained was often missing and only partial credit obtained for the question.
notes.3f: Only stronger candidates answered this fully correctly. Candidates were expected to take their gradient value G from (e) and record its value to a suitable number of significant figures for the experiment, which in this case was 2 or 3 significant figures.
